title: Energy resources and the National Grid
examTip: High potential difference → low current → less energy is dissipated by heating the cables (P = I²R). This is WHY the grid uses a high potential difference. Don't just say 'to save energy'. You need to explain the physics.
introTips: The National Grid uses a very high potential difference, up to 400,000 V. This cuts the energy wasted in cables.
Step-up transformers increase the potential difference. Step-down transformers decrease it.
Energy resources are used for transport, electricity generation and heating.
intro: When you plug something in, the electricity may have been made hundreds of miles away. It could come from a wind farm, a nuclear power station or a gas power station. Getting it to you without wasting most of it is a tricky engineering problem. The answer is to use a very high potential difference to send it a long way. Then the potential difference is stepped back down before it reaches your kettle. This is one of the cleverest uses of physics in everyday life.

keyPoints.heading: How the National Grid works
keyPoints.content: The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers. It runs from power stations to homes, schools and businesses. Electricity is generated at power stations at around 25,000 V (25 kV). A step-up transformer then raises the potential difference to up to 400,000 V (400 kV). This is for sending it a long way through transmission cables. At the other end, step-down transformers reduce the potential difference to a much lower value for homes. In homes it is 230 V. Why use such a high potential difference? Start from P = IV. Say the power (P) is fixed and the potential difference (V) is very high. Then the current (I) must be very low. Then use P_lost = I²R. A lower current means far less power wasted as heat in the resistance of the cables. Doubling the potential difference halves the current. Power loss ∝ I², so this cuts cable losses by four times.
writeBullets: National Grid — the network of cables and transformers carrying electricity across the UK
Generated at ~25 kV → stepped up to ~400 kV to send it a long way
Stepped down to 230 V for homes by step-down transformers
High potential difference → low current (P = IV, fixed P). I = P/V, so higher V means lower I
Low current → less power wasted as heat in cables: P_lost = I²R (power loss ∝ I²)

keyTerms.def: The network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to consumers across the UK
Power (W) = current (A) × potential difference (V); at constant power, higher V means lower I
Power wasted as heat in cables = current squared × resistance; lower current dramatically reduces heat loss

keyPoints.memTip: High V → low I → low I²R loss. The grid uses a high potential difference because cutting the current cuts cable losses by its square.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The I²R equation is the key to explaining WHY a high potential difference is used. Go beyond 'less energy is wasted'. Show why a lower current reduces heating losses. Try it without a calculator: 2 × 2 = 4, but 1 × 1 = 1. So halving the current cuts the heating loss to a quarter.

keyPoints.heading: Step-up and step-down transformers
keyPoints.content: Transformers change the potential difference in the National Grid. - A step-up transformer increases the potential difference. It is used between the power station and the transmission cables. - A step-down transformer decreases the potential difference. It is used between the transmission cables and homes. The high potential difference in the cables means a low current. So less energy is wasted by heating the cables.
writeBullets: Step-up transformer — increases the potential difference
Step-down transformer — decreases the potential difference
Step-up is used after the power station. Step-down is used before homes

keyTerms.def: A transformer that increases the potential difference
A transformer that decreases the potential difference

keyPoints.memTip: Step UP → potential difference goes up. Step DOWN → potential difference goes down.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Use the words 'potential difference', not 'voltage'. Say which transformer increases it and which decreases it.

keyPoints.heading: Energy resources and the environment
keyPoints.content: We use energy resources for transport, electricity generation and heating. For example, petrol and diesel fuel cars. Gas heats many homes. The UK uses a mix of energy resources. This balances reliability, cost and harm to the environment. A renewable resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used. Non-renewables: - Coal: releases more CO₂ than oil or gas for the same energy. CO₂ is a greenhouse gas. It adds to global warming and climate change. It is being phased out. - oil: used for transport fuels. Oil spills harm sea life. - Burning coal and oil also releases sulfur dioxide. This causes acid rain. - natural gas: less CO₂ than coal. It can be turned on quickly when demand rises. - nuclear fuel: no CO₂ while generating, and very reliable. But it makes radioactive waste. Renewables: - the Sun (solar cells): no emissions and quick to install. But it is intermittent. Solar cells work in daylight and less well when it is cloudy. They do not work at night. - wind: no emissions. But it is intermittent. - hydro-electricity: reliable, controllable and no emissions. But it needs rivers and dams, and affects ecosystems. - the tides: tides follow a regular cycle, so they are predictable. But barrages can damage habitats. - water waves: no emissions. But output depends on the weather, and it can disturb sea habitats. - geothermal: uses energy from hot rocks underground. It is reliable, but only works in a few places. - bio-fuel: made from plant or animal material. It may be carbon-neutral if crops regrow, but this is debated. Reliability: some resources are more reliable than others. Fossil fuels and nuclear are reliable. But nuclear power stations are slow to start up. Wind, solar and waves depend on the weather, so they are less reliable. Trends: coal use is falling. The use of renewable resources is rising. Science can identify environmental problems caused by using energy resources. But it cannot always solve them. This can be for political, social, ethical or economic reasons.
writeBullets: Uses of energy resources — transport, electricity generation and heating
Renewable — being (or able to be) replenished as it is used. Non-renewable — will run out
Coal and oil — release CO₂ and sulfur dioxide (acid rain). Oil spills harm sea life
Natural gas — less CO₂ than coal. Can be turned on quickly when demand rises
Nuclear fuel — no CO₂ while generating, very reliable. Makes radioactive waste
The Sun (solar cells) and wind — zero emissions. But intermittent (depends on weather)
Hydro-electricity — reliable, controllable, no emissions. Needs rivers and dams (affects ecosystems)
The tides — predictable, because tides follow a regular cycle. Barrages can damage habitats
Water waves — no emissions, but depends on the weather. Geothermal — reliable, but only in a few places
Bio-fuel — made from plant or animal material. May be carbon-neutral. How sustainable it is is debated
Trends — coal use is falling. Renewable use is rising
Science can identify environmental problems. It cannot always solve them, for political, social, ethical or economic reasons

keyTerms.def: An energy resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used — wind, solar, hydro, the tides, water waves, geothermal, bio-fuel
Energy resource that will run out — fossil fuels (coal, gas, oil) and nuclear (uranium)
Not always available — solar cells do not work at night, and wind turbines only work when the wind blows

keyPoints.memTip: Non-renewables are RELIABLE but produce CO₂ (or waste).
keyPoints.tutor_note: 6-mark questions often ask you to evaluate energy resources. Give both advantages AND disadvantages. Consider reliability, cost and harm to the environment.

0.question: Why does the National Grid transmit electricity at a very high potential difference (up to 400,000 V)?
options: A high potential difference means a lower current. This greatly reduces the power wasted as heat in the cables (P_lost = I²R)
A high potential difference makes the electricity travel faster through the cables
A high potential difference stops the cables overheating from solar radiation
A high potential difference is safer for the engineers who maintain the cables
0.correctFeedback: Exactly right! At constant power, a higher potential difference means a lower current (from P = IV). Lower current hugely reduces heating losses in the cables. This is because P_lost = I²R, so loss is proportional to current squared.
0.wrongFeedback: The answer is about cutting energy waste in the cables. From P = IV: higher potential difference → lower I. From P_lost = I²R: lower I → much less power wasted as heat. That is why the grid uses a high potential difference. It is not for speed, and not for safety.

1.question: What does a step-down transformer do in the National Grid?
options: It decreases the potential difference to a much lower value for homes
It increases the potential difference for the transmission cables
It generates electricity at the power station
It stores energy until it is needed
1.correctFeedback: Correct! A step-down transformer decreases the potential difference. This gives the much lower value used in homes.
1.wrongFeedback: Step-up transformers increase the potential difference. Step-down transformers decrease it to a much lower value for homes.

2.question: Why is wind a less reliable energy resource than nuclear fuel?
options: Wind turbines only work when the wind blows, so their output depends on the weather
Wind turbines release a lot of CO₂
Wind will run out one day
Wind turbines need uranium to work
2.correctFeedback: Correct! Wind is intermittent. Nuclear power does not depend on the weather, so it is reliable.
2.wrongFeedback: Wind is renewable and has no emissions. But it is intermittent: turbines only work when the wind blows. That makes it less reliable than nuclear.

commonMistakes: Saying the grid uses a high potential difference 'to save energy' without explaining how. Link it to P = IV (lower current) and P_lost = I²R (lower heating losses).
Mixing up step-up and step-down transformers. Step-up increases the potential difference. Step-down decreases it.
Saying the Sun is a renewable energy resource without saying it is intermittent. Give the advantage (no emissions). Give the disadvantage too (it depends on the weather).
Thinking renewable means 'free' or 'clean'. It means the resource is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.
examTips: For 'why a high potential difference in the grid' questions, say two things. (1) P = IV, so high V means low I. (2) P_lost = I²R, so low I means much less power wasted.
For 6-mark questions evaluating energy resources, give advantages AND disadvantages for each resource. Include reliability, harm to the environment and cost.
Some resources are more reliable than others. Say why, for example wind and solar depend on the weather.
